translation.text:
“Still,” I say[1], “sir, I will add another question.”

“Speak,” he says.

“I heard,” I say, “sir, from certain teachers, that there is no other repentance[a] except that one when we went down into the water and received forgiveness of our former sins.”[1][2]

He says to me, “You heard well; for so it is. For the one who has received forgiveness—”[3]

“Bear with me,” I say, “and make this clear to me also.”

“Speak,” he says.

“If a woman,” I say, “sir, or again some man, should fall asleep, and one of them marries[2], does the one who marries sin?”[4]

“He does not sin,” he says; “but if someone remains by himself,[5] he obtains for himself greater honor and great glory with the Lord; but if he also marries, he does not sin. Therefore keep chastity and modesty, and you will live to God. These things that I speak to you and am about to speak, keep from now on, from the day you were entrusted to me, and I will dwell in your house. And for your former trespasses there will be forgiveness, if you keep my commandments; and there will also be forgiveness for all[8][6][5][4][3], if they keep these commandments of mine and walk in this purity.”[6][8]

footnotes.text: “Repentance” here refers to the decisive turning associated with baptism, the release of former sins.
“We went down into the water” is early Christian language for baptism without naming it explicitly (cf. Didache 7).
The Greek is abrupt here (“For the one who has received forgiveness—”); many editors assume an interruption at this point.
“Fall asleep” is a common early Christian euphemism for dying.
“Chastity” could also be rendered “purity,” but the context favors sexual continence; “modesty” translates σεμνότης, moral gravity of comportment.
“Forgiveness” translates ἄφεσις; “remission” is a traditional alternative emphasizing release.

Repentance and related expressions are read in this works own context; they are not restricted to feeling sorry, and no uniform Godward formula is imposed. Use repentance for moral change while preserving the works own teaching about baptism, forgiveness, conduct and the angel of repentance; do not impose a different tradition on it.

“Still,” I say[1], “sir, I will add another question.”

“Speak,” he says.

“I heard,” I say, “sir, from certain teachers, that there is no other reorientation except that one when we went down into the water and received forgiveness of our former sins.”[1][2]

He says to me, “You heard well; for so it is. For the one who has received forgiveness—”[3]

“Bear with me,” I say, “and make this clear to me also.”

“Speak,” he says.

“If a woman,” I say, “sir, or again some man, should fall asleep, and one of them marries[2], does the one who marries sin?”[4]

“He does not sin,” he says; “but if someone remains by himself,[5] he obtains for himself greater honor and great glory with the Lord; but if he also marries, he does not sin. Therefore keep chastity and modesty, and you will live to God. These things that I speak to you and am about to speak, keep from now on, from the day you were entrusted to me, and I will dwell in your house. And for your former trespasses there will be forgiveness, if you keep my commandments; and there will also be forgiveness for all[8][6][5][4][3], if they keep these commandments of mine and walk in this purity.”[6][8]
